title: Rolling Stone Magazine
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of Rolling Stone magazine from its origins in San Francisco in the late 1960s, through its roots in the Ramparts magazine and the founding by Jann Wenner and Ralph Gleason, the first issue's cover and poor early sales, its growth, the move to New York, and its shifting focus toward pop culture and politics. They discuss new journalism and writers like Hunter S. Thompson, Tom Wolfe, and Cameron Crowe, Wenner's controversial management style, and a series of journalistic failures including the UVA rape article "A Rape on Campus," the bug chasers article, the Sean Penn interview with El Chapo, and recent pieces on Taylor Hawkins, Marilyn Manson, and Oklahoma ivermectin emergency rooms. The episode closes with a plug for Cream magazine and a listener mail email from Bethany in New Zealand.

segments.title: Opening banter and Cream magazine plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Josh's history with Rolling Stone and plug Cream magazine, which is back in print with archives access. They preview the history of Rolling Stone and Wenner's role.

segments.title: Ramparts and the counterculture origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe the San Francisco counterculture press and the influence of Ramparts magazine, including its 1968 cover offering reward money for information on cops who murdered black men, and its transformation under Warren Hinckle.

segments.title: Founding of Rolling Stone by Wenner and Gleason
segments.summary: Jann Wenner and jazz critic Ralph Gleason, who had worked at Ramparts, met at a Jefferson Airplane concert. Gleason left Ramparts after a falling out over a hippie critique, and the two hatched Rolling Stone, borrowing Ramparts staff, offices, paper and logo style. Jane Wenner's role is noted.

segments.title: First issue, John Lennon cover, and early sales
segments.summary: Rolling Stone's first issue was printed with about forty thousand copies and a John Lennon photo from How I Won the War on the cover. Most copies were returned, prompting a shift to outside distributors. The magazine later faced a name threat from the Rolling Stones, which was resolved.

segments.title: Wenner's management style and controversies
segments.summary: The hosts describe Wenner as a controlling and sometimes cruel editor who played labels and writers against each other, was criticized for sexism, and was known for under-the-table deals. His biography was difficult to produce. Discussion of his role in Rock and Roll Hall of Fame snubs and the Blowfish review dispute.
topics: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame snubs

segments.title: Circulation, format changes, and digital shift
segments.summary: Circulation peaked in 2008 at about 1.4 million and is now around 500,000. Wenner resisted digital publishing. The magazine changed page size several times, including a return to the larger format in 2018. The magazine moved from San Francisco to New York after Gleason's death.

segments.title: New journalism, Hunter S. Thompson, and notable writers
segments.summary: Rolling Stone was at the forefront of new journalism, with Hunter S. Thompson's gonzo work, including the Kentucky Derby piece and Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, and Tom Wolfe serialized work. Cameron Crowe, Ben Fong-Torres, Lester Bangs, and Joe Eszterhas also wrote for it.

segments.title: Rolling Stone journalistic controversies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 2014 UVA rape article by Sabrina Rubin Erdely, which was retracted after investigation found it unreliable, the 2003 bug chasers article with disputed doctor quotes, and the El Chapo profile by Sean Penn.

segments.title: Recent controversies and the shift toward speed
segments.summary: Recent Rolling Stone pieces drew criticism: a Taylor Hawkins article where quoted musicians disputed their context, a Marilyn Manson article presenting one-sided reporting, and an Oklahoma ivermectin emergency room story that was wrong. The hosts link this to a push for faster, more visceral journalism.

segments.title: Listener mail from Bethany
segments.summary: A listener from New Zealand, Bethany, writes that the show helps her daughters fall asleep. Josh and Chuck read the email and say hello to the girls, Thing One and Thing Two.
